03:12.120 --> 03:14.910
So you're gonna go into web driver,

03:14.910 --> 03:17.973
you're going to create a Chrome driver.

03:19.540 --> 03:21.760
Actually, you're just gonna create Chrome

03:22.680 --> 03:24.660
and now you need to put in here

03:24.660 --> 03:29.660
the executable path, difficult word to spell.

03:30.570 --> 03:35.160
This is just where your Chrome driver is saved.

03:35.160 --> 03:38.460
So since it's saved in the same directory

03:38.460 --> 03:40.140
as where we are now,

03:40.140 --> 03:42.240
basically I'm gonna copy paste this name

03:42.240 --> 03:45.600
and we're gonna say it's in the current directory

03:45.600 --> 03:48.030
and it's just this Chrome driver thing.

03:48.030 --> 03:49.530
This is what we need to point to.

03:49.530 --> 03:51.030
So it's right here.

03:51.030 --> 03:53.130
So we're saying it's in the current folder

03:53.130 --> 03:57.090
in the current directory and that's where it is.

03:57.090 --> 03:59.580
All right, so we've got our URL up here.

03:59.580 --> 04:02.010
So how do we do this using the Chrome driver now?

04:02.010 --> 04:04.620
So now we've created our driver.

04:04.620 --> 04:05.790
An important thing to do at the end

04:05.790 --> 04:08.670
is always to close the driver,

04:08.670 --> 04:10.620
very similar to closing a file,

04:10.620 --> 04:12.490
but here this is basically closing

04:15.060 --> 04:17.460
the Chrome app that we've opened.

04:17.460 --> 04:18.630
We'll leave this out for now

04:18.630 --> 04:21.000
just so that we can kind of go through everything,

04:21.000 --> 04:23.010
but it's always important to remember to close it

04:23.010 --> 04:23.843
or else you're just gonna have

04:23.843 --> 04:26.130
a bunch of Chrome applications running.

04:26.130 --> 04:30.217
So then we're going to say driver.get URL.

04:31.260 --> 04:33.660
Notice again, the syntax is very similar here.

04:33.660 --> 04:36.080
So now this is going to take our Chrome

04:36.080 --> 04:39.480
and it's going to load this URL

04:39.480 --> 04:42.300
and we can have the page source,

04:42.300 --> 04:45.390
which is the same thing as this r.text.

04:45.390 --> 04:47.340
We go into our driver

04:47.340 --> 04:51.210
and we look for the page source attribute.

04:51.210 --> 04:54.780
So that's gonna give us like that base HTML.

04:54.780 --> 04:57.510
All right, and then we can check

04:57.510 --> 04:59.610
basically copy pasting this

04:59.610 --> 05:02.820
and check if that value is in the page source

05:02.820 --> 05:05.340
that we used with the Chrome driver.

05:05.340 --> 05:07.470
So let's run this and then let's go through

05:07.470 --> 05:09.400
and compare what's actually going on.

05:09.400 --> 05:10.983
So we're gonna run this.

05:12.120 --> 05:14.310
First, we get no, they're using requests.

05:14.310 --> 05:16.410
And now what actually happens is

05:16.410 --> 05:19.140
Python is gonna open up a Chrome driver for us.

05:19.140 --> 05:22.620
And you can see that Chrome has actually been loaded

05:22.620 --> 05:24.480
and that's why we needed the Chrome driver.

05:24.480 --> 05:26.010
And all of this is automated.

05:26.010 --> 05:27.210
You can see up here,

05:27.210 --> 05:30.150
Chrome is being controlled by an automated test software.

05:30.150 --> 05:33.030
So you can see that Selenium is opening all this up for us.

05:33.030 --> 05:34.800
I'm of course, moving the mouse

05:34.800 --> 05:37.440
and it waits for this webpage to load

05:37.440 --> 05:39.720
or it has kind of a waiting time.

05:39.720 --> 05:43.290
And once the webpage is loaded, it gets the page source.

05:43.290 --> 05:44.880
And if we go back here,

05:44.880 --> 05:47.940
we see that the value is contained

05:47.940 --> 05:51.090
within the page source when we use Selenium,

05:51.090 --> 05:54.090
but it's not contained when we use requests.

05:54.090 --> 05:55.800
Now, the big difference here,

05:55.800 --> 05:57.420
and this time I'm gonna do the close

05:57.420 --> 05:59.340
so you can also see what happens when we close it

05:59.340 --> 06:01.560
'cause right now I just need to force quit it.

06:01.560 --> 06:04.110
Again, it's a Chrome application that opens.

06:04.110 --> 06:05.340
So again, we run it.

06:05.340 --> 06:06.210
Here we see no.

06:06.210 --> 06:08.310
Now we have a Chrome app opening.

06:08.310 --> 06:10.410
It loads the website

06:10.410 --> 06:12.990
and then it'll take the page source.

06:12.990 --> 06:14.400
And then once it's done with that,

06:14.400 --> 06:15.450
it's going to close it,

06:15.450 --> 06:18.750
which is gonna close the application that it opened.

06:18.750 --> 06:19.950
So you can see it's loading,

06:19.950 --> 06:21.960
then it's finished and it closes the application,

06:21.960 --> 06:23.850
which is why this is so important.

06:23.850 --> 06:25.380
Otherwise, you have to go

06:25.380 --> 06:29.040
and just close the new application yourself.

06:29.040 --> 06:31.650
So again, what happened is none of this stuff

06:31.650 --> 06:34.230
is part of the actual website.

06:34.230 --> 06:35.700
All of this stuff is loaded.

06:35.700 --> 06:37.950
And so that's why when we do requests,

06:37.950 --> 06:40.800
we basically just say, okay,

06:40.800 --> 06:42.030
I wanna access this website.

06:42.030 --> 06:46.020
You go there and you kind of get back the bare bones of it,

06:46.020 --> 06:47.310
but all of the stuff that's loaded,

06:47.310 --> 06:48.810
you're not gonna see with requests.

06:48.810 --> 06:50.480
So what Selenium allows us to do

06:50.480 --> 06:52.420
is we actually open a WebDriver.

06:52.420 --> 06:55.200
This WebDriver loads the website

06:55.200 --> 06:57.060
and then once it's loaded,

06:57.060 --> 07:01.290
we can then get the page source,

07:01.290 --> 07:03.120
which is kind of this updated HTML

07:03.120 --> 07:05.340
after all of the scripts and stuff have been run

07:05.340 --> 07:06.720
or after most of the scripts.

07:06.720 --> 07:08.400
That's something we'll get to later.

07:08.400 --> 07:12.600
And so we can see that this btc-usd,

07:12.600 --> 07:14.490
which is what we see here

07:14.490 --> 07:17.520
and which is what we also see when we inspect it here

07:17.520 --> 07:19.900
is found when we use Selenium

07:19.900 --> 07:23.010
and when we create this Chrome driver

07:23.010 --> 07:24.900
that kind of runs all of the stuff,

07:24.900 --> 07:27.870
but is not found when we use requests.

07:27.870 --> 07:30.330
So this is that dynamic part

07:30.330 --> 07:32.610
and a lot of websites now, of course,

07:32.610 --> 07:33.750
are becoming more dynamic

07:33.750 --> 07:36.060
and it's kind of a balance of having static elements,

07:36.060 --> 07:37.530
which is what this first part is,

07:37.530 --> 07:39.030
which is things that don't change.

07:39.030 --> 07:40.830
Static elements are good to have

07:40.830 --> 07:43.050
because they make your website load faster,

07:43.050 --> 07:45.120
but these things all kind of capture

07:45.120 --> 07:47.070
the things that are more interactive,

07:47.070 --> 07:50.250
which is also very common on modern websites,

07:50.250 --> 07:52.410
for one, because they look nicer with that

07:52.410 --> 07:53.400
to have them more interactive

07:53.400 --> 07:54.810
and also because people

07:54.810 --> 07:56.060
are getting faster internet connection

07:56.060 --> 08:00.900
so you can have more dynamic stuff on your website.

08:00.900 --> 08:03.360
So yeah, that's kind of the difference here.

08:03.360 --> 08:05.707
An important thing to note is you may ask,

08:05.707 --> 08:07.620
"Okay, why don't I always just use this?"

08:07.620 --> 08:10.200
Well, because you have to load the whole website here

08:10.200 --> 08:12.000
and you have to open the Chrome application

08:12.000 --> 08:13.890
and go to the URL and stuff,

08:13.890 --> 08:16.050
this actually also takes a bit longer.

08:16.050 --> 08:19.500
So if you can do it using the requests way,

08:19.500 --> 08:21.300
that's great because it will work faster,

08:21.300 --> 08:25.650
but sometimes you just can't find the information

08:25.650 --> 08:27.420
because it has to be loaded first.

08:27.420 --> 08:30.260
In those cases, you have to go and use Selenium

08:30.260 --> 08:33.020
so that you can interact with this website

08:33.020 --> 08:35.283
on a much deeper level.

whenever possible and everything else kind

03:07.890 --> 03:09.630
of supplement with the dynamic.

03:09.630 --> 03:11.580
But because the static works so much faster,

03:11.580 --> 03:14.640
and it's my opinion, much nicer to use, it's always good

03:14.640 --> 03:16.350
to see if it works with static first

03:16.350 --> 03:19.200
and only then go to the dynamic part.

03:19.200 --> 03:20.130
But yeah, we can see here

03:20.130 --> 03:22.323
that we can still get out the information that we need.

03:22.323 --> 03:25.290
We can do it using a similar approach.

03:25.290 --> 03:27.240
And of course, we can also get out different things

03:27.240 --> 03:30.363
like the attribute, for example, that we've seen here.

transcription:

00:00.300 --> 00:02.820
Max: Hey, everyone, it's Max. And welcome back.

00:02.820 --> 00:06.240
So in the last lecture, we used this sleep,

00:06.240 --> 00:08.250
essentially, as a little hack,

00:08.250 --> 00:10.920
so that our website has enough time,

00:10.920 --> 00:13.470
or our Chrome driver has enough time to load the website.

00:13.470 --> 00:15.690
But let's do this the Selenium way,

00:15.690 --> 00:18.120
because there are actually methods, part of Selenium,

00:18.120 --> 00:23.120
that we can use that will let us do all of this waiting.

00:23.880 --> 00:26.430
Okay, so the first thing that we can do

00:26.430 --> 00:31.430
is, let's just uncomment this, we can have an implicit wait.

00:33.030 --> 00:34.770
So we can go into our driver

00:34.770 --> 00:39.770
and set the implicit wait to 10 seconds.

00:41.280 --> 00:43.260
Now, this is usually set to zero seconds,

00:43.260 --> 00:45.720
but what this means is the driver will,

00:45.720 --> 00:47.310
while it's loading the website,

00:47.310 --> 00:50.190
it will basically wait up to 10 seconds

00:50.190 --> 00:53.790
for the website to finish loading.

00:53.790 --> 00:55.620
So let's try to do the same thing here,

00:55.620 --> 01:00.330
now, just replacing this time of sleep by an implicit wait,

01:00.330 --> 01:05.330
so letting the driver kind of wait a little bit longer,

01:05.460 --> 01:08.610
in this case, 10 seconds, for the website to finish loading

01:08.610 --> 01:12.090
rather than just making our program sleep.

01:12.090 --> 01:13.890
All right, so we can see, it didn't actually take

01:13.890 --> 01:15.060
all the way up to 10 seconds.

01:15.060 --> 01:17.940
Once it finished loading, then it continued on,

01:17.940 --> 01:20.910
and we got our data out from here.

01:20.910 --> 01:25.320
But yeah, so this is one way of going about the waiting.

01:25.320 --> 01:26.760
There's also something else that we can do,

01:26.760 --> 01:28.800
which is also extremely useful,

01:28.800 --> 01:31.620
which is waiting for specific elements

01:31.620 --> 01:33.660
to actually be visible on the page.

01:33.660 --> 01:34.950
So maybe sometimes we don't wanna wait

01:34.950 --> 01:35.970
for the whole page to load,

01:35.970 --> 01:37.920
we just need a specific element to be loaded

01:37.920 --> 01:40.260
so that we can interact with it.

01:40.260 --> 01:42.990
So yeah, let's go about doing that now.

01:42.990 --> 01:44.850
So the first thing that we're gonna wanna do

01:44.850 --> 01:48.437
is from selenium.webdriver.common,

01:51.330 --> 01:55.413
we're going to import,

01:56.640 --> 02:01.410
oop, that's a typo, by, oh, common.by.

02:01.410 --> 02:04.230
So this is just going to allow us to do this

02:04.230 --> 02:06.090
by XPath in a different way,

02:06.090 --> 02:09.690
which is kind of necessary for the syntax of the wait.

02:09.690 --> 02:11.370
So we'll see this all in action in a second.

02:11.370 --> 02:14.190
Let's just finish importing the rest of all of the modules.

02:14.190 --> 02:17.240
So this one's gonna be from selenium.webdriver.support.ui.

02:23.490 --> 02:26.130
We're going to import WebDriverWait.

02:29.880 --> 02:34.880
And then also, finally, from selenium.webdriver.support,

02:38.850 --> 02:43.670
we're going to import the expected conditions,

02:44.670 --> 02:47.340
and we're gonna shorthand this 'cause this is pretty long,

02:47.340 --> 02:50.280
and we'll just do that as lowercase es.

02:50.280 --> 02:54.330
Okay, so let's just go ahead and apply all these.

02:54.330 --> 02:58.680
You'll see why we needed each of these things in a second.

02:58.680 --> 03:00.900
All right, so the first thing that we're gonna define

03:00.900 --> 03:03.180
is a wait variable.

03:03.180 --> 03:05.707
So we're gonna use our WebDriverWait

03:07.470 --> 03:09.450
that we've just imported up here,

03:09.450 --> 03:12.630
and we're gonna put as input here our driver,

03:12.630 --> 03:14.070
and another parameter

03:14.070 --> 03:17.640
is gonna be the time that we allow the waiting.

03:17.640 --> 03:22.290
So it's gonna be the time that it's allowed to load for,

03:22.290 --> 03:24.300
which we'll set to 10 seconds.

03:24.300 --> 03:27.540
So we put that in here, make that a bit more dynamic.

03:27.540 --> 03:30.780
All right, so we've defined our WebDriverWait

03:30.780 --> 03:33.120
for this specific driver,

03:33.120 --> 03:35.100
and basically, it can then wait

03:35.100 --> 03:38.520
up to the amount of time that we have here.

03:38.520 --> 03:43.500
Okay, so let's just do this for one element for now.

03:43.500 --> 03:47.670
So we're gonna take this part, copy this out.

03:47.670 --> 03:51.690
So this is usually done within a try and except statement,

03:51.690 --> 03:53.550
so that if the time expires

03:53.550 --> 03:55.170
and the element still hasn't loaded,

03:55.170 --> 03:57.630
your program doesn't crash, but you can just continue on.

03:57.630 --> 04:01.440
So we're gonna do try to wait for the following to load,

04:01.440 --> 04:03.060
and except if it doesn't work,

04:03.060 --> 04:05.490
we're just going to pass for now.

04:05.490 --> 04:10.410
We can no longer use I, so we'll just put in here 1 again.

04:10.410 --> 04:11.243
All right.

04:11.243 --> 04:14.340
So we're gonna use this wait variable

04:14.340 --> 04:15.173
that we've created now.

04:15.173 --> 04:16.410
So we're gonna say, all right,

04:16.410 --> 04:19.110
so let's actually do the waiting.

04:19.110 --> 04:22.803
So we're gonna do the wait until,

04:26.070 --> 04:28.020
and then we're gonna wait until,

04:28.020 --> 04:30.870
and we're gonna use the expected conditions.

04:30.870 --> 04:33.210
And here, we're gonna go into

04:33.210 --> 04:38.210
the visibility of element located.

04:42.720 --> 04:47.693
And we're going to look at this by XPath,

04:49.590 --> 04:54.590
and the XPath that we're gonna look for is this one here.

04:55.140 --> 04:59.043
So we'll just put that one up there.

05:00.390 --> 05:01.320
All right.

05:01.320 --> 05:05.010
So we've got the wait statement here,

05:05.010 --> 05:08.190
which basically says, okay, using this WebDriverWait,

05:08.190 --> 05:11.670
which applies to our driver that we've created up here,

05:11.670 --> 05:14.523
which says you can wait up to 10 seconds,

05:15.870 --> 05:17.220
make sure the indentation is correct.

05:17.220 --> 05:19.110
We're going to wait until,

05:19.110 --> 05:23.820
and then we'll use the expected conditions

05:23.820 --> 05:25.830
and just using the method in here

05:25.830 --> 05:29.220
called visibility of element located.

05:29.220 --> 05:34.127
So we're gonna wait until the following element is visible

05:34.127 --> 05:38.073
and we're going to identify that element using the XPath.

05:39.150 --> 05:42.810
Oh, supposed to do ESC not EC.

05:42.810 --> 05:47.670
Okay. So if we type in dot vis, yep.

05:47.670 --> 05:50.640
All right. So the expected condition.

05:50.640 --> 05:53.493
Actually, makes a lot more sense as EC.

05:54.600 --> 05:56.490
And to make sure we get that right, we can just type in.

05:56.490 --> 06:00.840
Yep. So we see we've already got it suggested to us.

06:00.840 --> 06:04.860
Visibility of element located.

06:04.860 --> 06:08.130
So that tells us that the import went correctly.

06:08.130 --> 06:11.400
So we're going to, again,

06:11.400 --> 06:13.860
define a load time of up to 10 seconds,

06:13.860 --> 06:16.200
and we're gonna create this WebDriverWait class,

06:16.200 --> 06:18.750
which applies to our driver here,

06:18.750 --> 06:20.940
our Chrome driver that we've created up here,

06:20.940 --> 06:23.970
and it lets it load for up to the following amount.

06:23.970 --> 06:25.410
And then we're gonna say, all right,

06:25.410 --> 06:28.140
so we're going to wait until

06:28.140 --> 06:31.830
the following element is visible,

06:31.830 --> 06:36.330
and that element is gonna be determined by the XPath,

06:36.330 --> 06:41.330
and, well, it's this XPath that it's going to wait for.

06:41.820 --> 06:45.090
And yeah, if that works,

06:45.090 --> 06:48.453
then we're going to print out this element,

06:50.160 --> 06:51.420
and if it doesn't work,

06:51.420 --> 06:53.760
then we're just going to, well, not do anything.

06:53.760 --> 06:57.750
Or we can put an exception here and say, Exception as E,

06:57.750 --> 07:00.600
if we want, we can print out our exception,

07:00.600 --> 07:05.010
or we can print out "Element not visible,"

07:05.010 --> 07:06.603
or something like that.

07:07.650 --> 07:09.660
All right. Let's go ahead and run this.

07:09.660 --> 07:11.673
Let's see if this works.

07:18.300 --> 07:19.170
Okay.

07:19.170 --> 07:20.760
So what we have in this case

07:20.760 --> 07:23.400
is it looks like we actually have a dash here.

07:23.400 --> 07:24.960
First of all, we can remove this pass

07:24.960 --> 07:27.270
because we are doing something here,

07:27.270 --> 07:29.130
so the pass is no longer necessary.

07:29.130 --> 07:30.840
Let's comment this out again

07:30.840 --> 07:33.090
to stop the Chrome diver from closing.

07:33.090 --> 07:34.890
And let's pay special attention to what's happening

07:34.890 --> 07:37.530
because these are issues that you can encounter

07:37.530 --> 07:40.350
when the internet speed is kind of low.

07:40.350 --> 07:41.820
So if we look here, we can see

07:41.820 --> 07:43.500
that there's actually a dash loaded

07:43.500 --> 07:45.570
right before the prices are filled in.

07:45.570 --> 07:48.780
And our condition works

07:48.780 --> 07:51.000
because it's waiting for the element to be located.

07:51.000 --> 07:53.580
However, the element isn't completely filled in yet,

07:53.580 --> 07:55.320
so we're not actually getting the information

07:55.320 --> 07:57.270
that we want from it.

07:57.270 --> 08:01.320
So we can comment this out again and let's try to do that,

08:01.320 --> 08:03.300
let's try to kind of get around this.

08:03.300 --> 08:05.730
So right now, if we're in here,

08:05.730 --> 08:08.220
we're waiting for this to show up,

08:08.220 --> 08:10.230
but maybe let's be a bit more specific.

08:10.230 --> 08:15.230
Let's go into here, the second TD tag,

08:17.370 --> 08:22.370
and we'll go into this P tag here

08:22.860 --> 08:25.923
and we'll wait specifically for this element to show up.

08:28.440 --> 08:32.220
All right. So let's try running that one more time.

08:32.220 --> 08:33.633
See what happens this time.

08:40.860 --> 08:41.693
All right.

08:41.693 --> 08:45.993
So we've got, well, we've got the element.

08:48.210 --> 08:49.770
We've now loaded. (chuckles)

08:49.770 --> 08:52.080
We've correctly waited for the element to load.

08:52.080 --> 08:55.980
However, because we're specifying this XPath,

08:55.980 --> 08:58.740
we now have to, well, change these up a little bit.

08:58.740 --> 09:02.190
This can be, copy this down here.

09:02.190 --> 09:04.560
This can be our load XPath,

09:04.560 --> 09:07.200
which is gonna be what we're going to want

09:07.200 --> 09:09.450
for our web driver to load for.

09:09.450 --> 09:13.260
And our data XPath is going to be the same thing,

09:13.260 --> 09:14.970
just removing that.

09:14.970 --> 09:17.850
So we're doing this because before we saw

09:17.850 --> 09:21.930
that if we just wait for this element to load here,

09:21.930 --> 09:23.790
or, sorry, for this element to load,

09:23.790 --> 09:26.520
then we actually get a dash here before the data is filled,

09:26.520 --> 09:28.710
and so there are two loading things that happen.

09:28.710 --> 09:30.240
So to make sure we get data,

09:30.240 --> 09:33.270
we're gonna wait for this change,

09:33.270 --> 09:34.860
this percentage change down here to load,

09:34.860 --> 09:37.350
because this will probably be a dash beforehand.

09:37.350 --> 09:38.640
So we're gonna wait specifically

09:38.640 --> 09:40.410
for this percentage change to load,

09:40.410 --> 09:42.060
which is this thing down here.

09:42.060 --> 09:44.760
But we actually wanna extract data from this whole block,

09:44.760 --> 09:46.153
so we're gonna have a different XPath,

09:46.153 --> 09:48.900
we're just gonna define what's loaded,

09:48.900 --> 09:50.340
and then we're gonna have the other one,

09:50.340 --> 09:53.670
which is where we're going to extract the data from.

09:53.670 --> 09:55.863
So if we run this one more time,

09:56.820 --> 10:00.000
and here, we can see again, the dash kind of shows up,

10:00.000 --> 10:02.340
and now, these values show up.

10:02.340 --> 10:03.780
And yep, there we go.

10:03.780 --> 10:07.560
So now, we've finally kind of gotten back to what we wanted,

10:07.560 --> 10:10.470
and we've got the other way of waiting

10:10.470 --> 10:12.450
for specific things to load,

10:12.450 --> 10:14.700
which is defining this WebDriverWait

10:14.700 --> 10:17.070
for our web driver that we're using,

10:17.070 --> 10:21.300
saying you can load for up to this long,

10:21.300 --> 10:23.250
and then we're gonna say, "All right, web driver,

10:23.250 --> 10:27.420
wait until you see the following element loaded."

10:27.420 --> 10:30.960
And here, we actually had to define a deeper element,

10:30.960 --> 10:33.210
this one, which is something that only gets loaded

10:33.210 --> 10:34.680
after the price has been loaded,

10:34.680 --> 10:35.700
which is something that we found

10:35.700 --> 10:37.470
just by experimenting around.

10:37.470 --> 10:38.850
We say, all right, wait for that.

10:38.850 --> 10:40.620
But again, the data that we wanna extract

10:40.620 --> 10:43.203
is from this path here.

10:44.100 --> 10:47.160
So yeah, this is how we can use an explicit wait,

10:47.160 --> 10:49.740
whereas above here, we used an implicit wait.

10:49.740 --> 10:53.550
And you can, usually, first try with the implicit wait,

10:53.550 --> 10:56.220
but then when you want to, specifically,

10:56.220 --> 10:58.290
when the implicit wait is not doing what you want it to,

10:58.290 --> 11:01.110
and the element that you're looking for is still not there,

11:01.110 --> 11:03.510
which could be the case like we encountered

11:03.510 --> 11:06.210
for that dash showing up instead of the actual number,

11:06.210 --> 11:09.033
you may have to do an explicit wait instead.

11:10.320 --> 11:12.630
So yeah, these are the kind of two options that you have.

11:12.630 --> 11:14.790
And the really nice thing about this

11:14.790 --> 11:18.480
is that rather than making your program sleep

11:18.480 --> 11:20.700
or pause for a certain amount of time,

11:20.700 --> 11:24.330
you're giving it a range of time that it can wait for,

11:24.330 --> 11:27.630
and if it finds the element before that time is up,

11:27.630 --> 11:28.590
it will just continue on.

11:28.590 --> 11:31.380
So it won't wait the full duration, which is important,

11:31.380 --> 11:33.090
because, otherwise, if you're always waiting

11:33.090 --> 11:34.920
for a specific amount of time,

11:34.920 --> 11:36.600
then your program's really gonna,

11:36.600 --> 11:37.890
you know, it's gonna be much slower

11:37.890 --> 11:40.920
if it's always waiting for 10 seconds not doing anything.

11:40.920 --> 11:44.310
And this allows that loading to happen dynamically,

11:44.310 --> 11:45.420
which, of course, is much better

11:45.420 --> 11:48.090
because it will speed up your program

11:48.090 --> 11:50.160
and you can also deal with,

11:50.160 --> 11:51.870
in case the element wasn't found,

11:51.870 --> 11:53.670
what are you gonna do in that case?

11:53.670 --> 11:55.230
And dealing with these sort of things

11:55.230 --> 11:56.400
and keeping these things in mind

11:56.400 --> 11:57.900
is important for web scrappers,

11:57.900 --> 12:02.460
especially if your internet connection may be variable,

12:02.460 --> 12:03.960
then it's important to keep in mind

12:03.960 --> 12:05.820
like loading limitations.

12:05.820 --> 12:09.780
But also, if you're creating web scrappers for other people

12:09.780 --> 12:12.720
or if it's for the organization that you work for

12:12.720 --> 12:14.040
and you're putting it online,

12:14.040 --> 12:16.680
network conditions can be different for other places.

12:16.680 --> 12:18.660
So even though things may be running smoothly for you,

12:18.660 --> 12:20.580
if you have insanely fast internet,

12:20.580 --> 12:22.590
that may not be the case for other people.

12:22.590 --> 12:25.710
And so it's important to take care of loading,

12:25.710 --> 12:29.130
especially for the important elements that contain your data

12:29.130 --> 12:32.703
or other things that you wanna do, like navigations,

12:33.870 --> 12:36.420
which is something that we'll also see a bit later.

12:36.420 --> 12:37.710
Keeping all that stuff in mind,

12:37.710 --> 12:40.290
you know that some people are limited by network

12:40.290 --> 12:42.630
or some areas are limited by network,

12:42.630 --> 12:44.430
when you're hosting it somewhere

12:44.430 --> 12:47.400
or passing it on to other people and letting them run it,

12:47.400 --> 12:51.480
so making or adding these explicit waiting things

12:51.480 --> 12:55.230
to make sure that the data actually shows up

12:55.230 --> 12:56.820
before your program guards this stuff,

12:56.820 --> 12:57.677
is insanely important.

12:57.677 --> 12:59.280
'Cause otherwise, if you go back

12:59.280 --> 13:01.410
and like look at the data even a week later,

13:01.410 --> 13:02.880
and you notice that everything

13:02.880 --> 13:04.500
is filled in with these dashes

13:04.500 --> 13:06.810
because there wasn't enough time for the data to load,

13:06.810 --> 13:07.650
that would really suck

13:07.650 --> 13:09.630
because you've let this program run for a week

13:09.630 --> 13:11.850
and you thought you'd have data by now, but you don't.

13:11.850 --> 13:15.030
So taking care of all of these nuances

13:15.030 --> 13:18.663
is also a very important part of web scrapping.

course_name: Web Scraping In Python: Master The Fundamentals

transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.270 --> 00:02.910
Max: Hey everyone, it's Max and welcome back.

00:02.910 --> 00:04.320
So in the previous lecture,

00:04.320 --> 00:06.810
we saw how we went about adding

00:06.810 --> 00:08.640
explicit and implicit weights

00:08.640 --> 00:13.290
so that our browser can kind of load these things

00:13.290 --> 00:14.760
more dynamically.

00:14.760 --> 00:17.040
Now, something that you may have noticed by now is,

00:17.040 --> 00:19.530
all right, so if we run this,

00:19.530 --> 00:21.630
then our browser is gonna open.

00:21.630 --> 00:23.460
Now this is kind of nice for now,

00:23.460 --> 00:25.170
because it allows us to do like debugging

00:25.170 --> 00:27.360
and allows us to see what's going on.

00:27.360 --> 00:29.910
But once our web scrapper is actually loading,

00:29.910 --> 00:32.070
if we want to have a web scrapper running in the background,

00:32.070 --> 00:35.130
we don't want to continuously have like a Chrome app

00:35.130 --> 00:36.420
popping up or something like that,

00:36.420 --> 00:38.070
just popping into the foreground.

00:38.070 --> 00:40.650
So this is really nice for debugging

00:40.650 --> 00:43.080
and making sure things work

00:43.080 --> 00:45.270
and just seeing what's going on live,

00:45.270 --> 00:46.920
how the loading is going.

00:46.920 --> 00:50.040
But then we also want to remove this,

00:50.040 --> 00:51.870
like once things are working correctly,

00:51.870 --> 00:54.240
it'd be better if it doesn't pop up.

00:54.240 --> 00:58.590
Now doing that is called making the driver headless.

00:58.590 --> 01:01.800
So to do that, it's actually pretty easy,

01:01.800 --> 01:04.470
we're gonna define some options.

01:04.470 --> 01:08.493
We're going to go into webdriver.ChromeOptions.

01:11.790 --> 01:15.060
So webdriver imported from Selenium here.

01:15.060 --> 01:17.940
And then we're going to go into our options

01:17.940 --> 01:22.940
and we're gonna say, add_argument ("headless"), like this.

01:24.270 --> 01:28.927
And then in here we can just say options=options.

01:31.650 --> 01:35.070
And what you'll notice is that the webdriver

01:35.070 --> 01:36.120
no longer pops up.

01:36.120 --> 01:37.620
And if you run this on your end,

01:37.620 --> 01:39.960
you're gonna see that the application is gonna open

01:39.960 --> 01:42.540
for just a split second, and then it's gonna go away again.

01:42.540 --> 01:46.560
And so now what we've done is the application still opens,

01:46.560 --> 01:48.240
the Chrome driver still opens,

01:48.240 --> 01:50.520
but it's running in headless mode is what it's called.

01:50.520 --> 01:54.197
So there's no UI going on with it, which is really nice

01:54.197 --> 01:56.610
when we just want to let this run

01:56.610 --> 01:58.830
and we don't want to be disturbed by it,

01:58.830 --> 02:00.270
and things popping up.

02:00.270 --> 02:04.567
And also loading the driver, loading the visual elements

02:04.567 --> 02:06.210
and displaying it on the screen

02:06.210 --> 02:09.540
also takes up computational resources and memory.

02:09.540 --> 02:11.520
And so the best thing to do

02:11.520 --> 02:14.190
when you have this web scrapper completed

02:14.190 --> 02:17.700
is to make sure that your webdriver becomes headless

02:17.700 --> 02:20.190
so that this application is kind of hidden

02:20.190 --> 02:23.490
and it's still running and it's still doing the same things,

02:23.490 --> 02:27.450
it's just now the application doesn't pop up anymore.

02:27.450 --> 02:31.980
And then it's much nicer because ultimately,

02:31.980 --> 02:33.900
that's much more scalable

02:33.900 --> 02:36.490
and it's also just much less intrusive

02:37.590 --> 02:40.350
and also what you expect from a program, right?

02:40.350 --> 02:43.260
That not things are popping up all over the place,

02:43.260 --> 02:46.623
rather that things are hidden and they're running,

02:47.940 --> 02:51.693
but they're not kind of overtaking your screen.

05:51.408 --> 05:54.032
as this web driver is open and running,

05:54.032 --> 05:56.462

06:01.410 --> 06:04.243

06:04.243 --> 06:06.690

06:06.690 --> 06:08.135
with the static thing.

06:08.135 --> 06:11.100
But of course they each have their trade-offs

06:11.100 --> 06:13.516

06:13.516 --> 06:18.270
but we're getting it from a chart

06:18.270 --> 06:19.920
that's actually made for something else.

06:19.920 --> 06:23.040
So probably not the best place to get this price from.

06:23.040 --> 06:26.280
You can probably just get it from a different website

06:26.280 --> 06:28.200
where you can get the data statically

06:28.200 --> 06:30.120
and that way things will work a little bit quicker

06:30.120 --> 06:32.520
and you don't have to continuously have a web driver running

06:32.520 --> 06:35.440
in the background, which still takes up memory

06:35.440 --> 06:37.892
and CPU power and everything like that.

06:37.892 --> 06:41.537
So like I said before, if you can find a way to

06:41.537 --> 06:44.276
get it statically, then it's better.

06:44.276 --> 06:48.300
But of course as we can see dynamic are always options

06:48.300 --> 06:50.224
and they also still work really nicely.

06:50.224 --> 06:54.419
And a lot of it is much more about making sure

06:54.419 --> 06:57.079
that your things run generally

06:57.079 --> 07:00.570
and that things are staying general,

07:00.570 --> 07:02.160
that things aren't crashing.

07:02.160 --> 07:05.893
And also just being aware

07:05.893 --> 07:08.580
that like things may change

07:08.580 --> 07:10.200
and just making sure that the data

07:10.200 --> 07:13.050
that you have is actually being saved, right?

07:13.050 --> 07:14.970
At the end of the day, the thing that you want

07:14.970 --> 07:17.010
with web scrapping is you want the data

07:17.010 --> 07:18.600
and you want it to be saved.

07:18.600 --> 07:19.860
And so that's what you're looking for

07:19.860 --> 07:22.110
and whatever approach gets you there, as long

07:22.110 --> 07:23.850
as it works relatively quickly so

07:23.850 --> 07:25.470
that you can update your data

07:25.470 --> 07:26.892
at whatever intervals you want.

07:26.892 --> 07:29.670
And as long as it doesn't, well

07:29.670 --> 07:31.680
ideally it doesn't take up too much memory

07:31.680 --> 07:32.744
or too much processing so

07:32.744 --> 07:35.267
that things don't become like too expensive

07:35.267 --> 07:37.500
to run either in terms of time

07:37.500 --> 07:38.910
because you have to wait for your computer

07:38.910 --> 07:41.940
to do other things or also just in terms of paying

07:41.940 --> 07:44.310
for electricity or all those sorts of things.

07:44.310 --> 07:45.476
So those are things to consider.

07:45.476 --> 07:47.695
But of course the objective

07:47.695 --> 07:50.550
with web scrapping firsthand is just to make sure

07:50.550 --> 07:52.099
that the data that you're looking for

07:52.099 --> 07:54.480
is something that you can actually get.

07:54.480 --> 07:56.871
And the nice thing is once you have these web scrappers,

07:56.871 --> 07:59.490
unless you know they change,

07:59.490 --> 08:01.110
like the developers change the website,

08:01.110 --> 08:03.442
in which case you're gonna have to adapt your web scrapper

08:03.442 --> 08:04.886
to the new website format,

08:04.886 --> 08:06.810
you can just let these run

08:06.810 --> 08:09.218
and it'll continue to pull information from it, save data

08:09.218 --> 08:12.162
for you, which you can then use.

08:12.162 --> 08:14.635
So now you have a continuous source of data,

08:14.635 --> 08:16.665
but of course it requires monitoring

08:16.665 --> 08:20.162
because websites change, things change.

08:20.162 --> 08:25.162
So it's always good to set up things to help you monitor.

08:25.230 --> 08:26.967
Either you can do the monitoring manually,

08:26.967 --> 08:29.820
check it once a day, every couple of days,

08:29.820 --> 08:33.708
once a week, up to you how often this program is being run

08:33.708 --> 08:36.690
or if you run it manually you can check to make sure

08:36.690 --> 08:38.040
that things work correctly just

08:38.040 --> 08:39.487
to see if all the fields are filled out.

08:39.487 --> 08:44.219
Otherwise you can also look at libraries

08:44.219 --> 08:46.530
that let you send email notifications to yourself

08:46.530 --> 08:49.110
or you can think of other ways of how you want

08:49.110 --> 08:52.608
to be alerted when missing values start coming in.

08:52.608 --> 08:56.712
And of course, always make sure to think about load times

08:56.712 --> 08:58.860
and if the load time is not enough,

08:58.860 --> 09:00.837
you can also up this right, you can up this to 30 seconds,

09:00.837 --> 09:05.550
you can up it longer because some places will have much

09:05.550 --> 09:06.720
faster network connection,

09:06.720 --> 09:08.880
especially if you're creating these things on

09:08.880 --> 09:11.100
interconnect connections that are faster.

09:11.100 --> 09:13.488
You want to make sure that things don't stop working

09:13.488 --> 09:17.820
when your web scrapper is run some way

09:17.820 --> 09:20.523
where the internet connection is a bit slower.

transcription:
WEBVTT

00:00.330 --> 00:01.950
Max: Hey everyone, it's Max and welcome back

00:01.950 --> 00:05.220
to our data extraction tutorial that we've done in Python.

00:05.220 --> 00:08.220
So we're pretty much done with the data extraction part

00:08.220 --> 00:11.010
that we did when we crawled websites

00:11.010 --> 00:12.840
and then we parsed through the HTML code,

00:12.840 --> 00:15.480
and we got all of our data out like that.

00:15.480 --> 00:16.770
And we used the request library

00:16.770 --> 00:19.680
to which I have open right here.

00:19.680 --> 00:22.470
So one more thing that I would like to touch on,

00:22.470 --> 00:24.930
but I'm not gonna go into too much detail just

00:24.930 --> 00:28.350
because I have a another course devoted to this

00:28.350 --> 00:32.940
that uses APIs and also has practical example

00:32.940 --> 00:36.240
or a worked example of you know, setting up API calls

00:36.240 --> 00:38.490
and how to parse all of that data.

00:38.490 --> 00:41.580
But nevertheless, I still wanna show you

00:41.580 --> 00:44.670
that all of this is possible or what exactly an API is.

00:44.670 --> 00:47.100
So we'll just start off,

00:47.100 --> 00:50.970
and there are many different services that have APIs.

00:50.970 --> 00:53.250
So usually a lot of big websites,

00:53.250 --> 00:56.190
and I've pulled up two examples here.

00:56.190 --> 00:57.480
One of them is PayPal,

00:57.480 --> 00:59.940
and the other one would be an OpenWeather map.

00:59.940 --> 01:02.280
But you know, YouTube for example, or Facebook,

01:02.280 --> 01:06.000
or all of the kind of standard web services that you know,

01:06.000 --> 01:09.003
or websites probably have an API included.

01:09.840 --> 01:11.280
So an API again stands

01:11.280 --> 01:13.650
for the application programming interface.

01:13.650 --> 01:15.090
And the reason that they have that is

01:15.090 --> 01:17.760
because it allows you to very easily integrate

01:17.760 --> 01:21.090
their services into a new product that you're building.

01:21.090 --> 01:24.330
So for them, it's also a very big advantage to have an API

01:24.330 --> 01:27.720
because it allows them to spread their product in some sense

01:27.720 --> 01:29.940
and you can just do whatever you want with it

01:29.940 --> 01:31.950
and integrate their services

01:31.950 --> 01:34.110
into whatever it is that you're building.

01:34.110 --> 01:36.480
However, an API really does

01:36.480 --> 01:38.220
have a lot of cool things with it.

01:38.220 --> 01:41.280
So one thing that we noticed when we scrapped data is

01:41.280 --> 01:43.620
that it was kind of tedious at times

01:43.620 --> 01:46.740
to just go through the HTML and look for exactly

01:46.740 --> 01:49.290
what it is that we wanted to find, identify patterns,

01:49.290 --> 01:51.960
and use all of that to extract some data.

01:51.960 --> 01:55.290
And APIs make it a lot, a lot easier for us.

01:55.290 --> 01:59.670
So what APIs do is they're kind of a standard way

01:59.670 --> 02:01.380
of talking to a web service.

02:01.380 --> 02:05.878
And we'll just look here at the example of

02:05.878 --> 02:07.830
the OpenWeather map and there's usually

02:07.830 --> 02:10.860
a base URL that you talk to.

02:10.860 --> 02:13.200
In this case, it would be for example the API dot

02:13.200 --> 02:16.650
and then the website name and then some special format.

02:16.650 --> 02:18.810
And then in here you include some

02:18.810 --> 02:19.920
of the core requests that you want.

02:19.920 --> 02:21.750
So in this case, the weather for London.

02:21.750 --> 02:25.500
And, so you pass all of that in a URL to a special website

02:25.500 --> 02:29.010
that usually has an API within it

02:29.010 --> 02:32.820
or the API kind of the API is part

02:32.820 --> 02:36.510
of is like a sub-domain in some sense of of the URL.

02:36.510 --> 02:40.710
And so, that makes your get request

02:40.710 --> 02:43.440
usually go to directly to this API call.

02:43.440 --> 02:46.020
And that gives you back a structured data.

02:46.020 --> 02:49.920
So if we click on this example here, then once this loads,

02:49.920 --> 02:52.200
this is the data that we're gonna be getting back.

02:52.200 --> 02:56.280
And this looks very similar to a Python dictionary.

02:56.280 --> 02:58.500
The format is actually called JSON Format,

02:58.500 --> 03:01.830
so it's a JavaScript object notation,

03:01.830 --> 03:05.130
but it looks very similar to a Python dictionary,

03:05.130 --> 03:08.460
and we can also access data in exactly the same way.

03:08.460 --> 03:09.840
And so, this is the type of data

03:09.840 --> 03:14.190
that we would be getting back if we'd be talking to APIs.

03:14.190 --> 03:15.900
And that makes it a lot easier

03:15.900 --> 03:17.820
because everything is structured for us,

03:17.820 --> 03:19.290
it's nicely laid out,

03:19.290 --> 03:21.960
and we can just go into whatever key that we want

03:21.960 --> 03:23.970
and pull out the relevant information,

03:23.970 --> 03:27.510
rather than having to parse everything for ourselves.

03:27.510 --> 03:30.480
Now, every API, of course, is a little bit different.

03:30.480 --> 03:32.460
So here, we've got weather data, you know,

03:32.460 --> 03:34.920
if you're looking at maybe a finance API

03:34.920 --> 03:37.980
or something, you'll get back some finance data,

03:37.980 --> 03:39.810
or if you're looking at, I don't know,

03:39.810 --> 03:41.700
some science stuff like earthquakes,

03:41.700 --> 03:43.650
then you could be getting frequency data,

03:43.650 --> 03:44.880
and all of that stuff.

03:44.880 --> 03:46.890
So depending on the API that you're using,

03:46.890 --> 03:49.410
the data that you're gonna be getting back

03:49.410 --> 03:50.550
will be different.

03:50.550 --> 03:53.190
The keys will be different and the values obviously too.

03:53.190 --> 03:55.530
However, the general format, this JSON format

03:55.530 --> 03:58.230
is very standard and there's another format

03:58.230 --> 04:01.470
that's called XML which is a little bit less used,

04:01.470 --> 04:02.700
but it's also very standard.

04:02.700 --> 04:04.800
It looks in some sense similar

04:04.800 --> 04:08.220
to HTML code in some sense,

04:08.220 --> 04:11.490
just that little bit with the greater than

04:11.490 --> 04:13.350
and less than symbols and everything.

04:13.350 --> 04:16.230
But it's standard ways to organize data.

04:16.230 --> 04:20.460
And Python can very easily read these data formats,

04:20.460 --> 04:22.680
so that's what APIs are all about.

04:22.680 --> 04:27.330
They're about making access to data a lot easier.

04:27.330 --> 04:30.810
And you can see here that the general format, for example,

04:30.810 --> 04:32.970
would be just to put in these input parameters

04:32.970 --> 04:35.610
and then you just get back exactly what it is

04:35.610 --> 04:36.990
that you're looking for,

04:36.990 --> 04:38.520
and you don't have to go through everything

04:38.520 --> 04:40.950
and parse it, you just ask the web service directly,

04:40.950 --> 04:44.010
hey, this is what I want, and they're like, no problem.

04:44.010 --> 04:46.350
And they put it all together in a little package,

04:46.350 --> 04:48.930
and they send you back the data.

04:48.930 --> 04:51.390
And so, what we see here in requests

04:51.390 --> 04:53.240
when we actually open up the website,

04:54.300 --> 04:55.920
this is actually an API call now.

04:55.920 --> 04:57.930
We've used requests and especially,

04:57.930 --> 05:02.100
the get request to perform calls,

05:02.100 --> 05:03.660
so that we can open a website,

05:03.660 --> 05:06.990
and we've looked at the text usually,

05:06.990 --> 05:10.500
but you can also use the same get request method

05:10.500 --> 05:13.140
for APIs like we see done here.

05:13.140 --> 05:14.457
And usually for APIs,

05:14.457 --> 05:17.220
you also have a form of authentication.

05:17.220 --> 05:20.460
So either they would provide you with an API key,

05:20.460 --> 05:23.130
in which case, you would pass that as the authentication,

05:23.130 --> 05:25.860
or you have a standard username and password.

05:25.860 --> 05:27.480
This is a little bit less common

05:27.480 --> 05:29.130
because you usually don't wanna provide

05:29.130 --> 05:30.960
your raw username and password.

05:30.960 --> 05:33.150

00:26.390 --> 00:27.770

01:14.550 --> 01:19.260
First, notice the dot over here in regular expression syntax.

01:19.260 --> 01:26.700
The Dot is a special character matching any character, no matter if it's a letter, a digit, a whitespace,

01:26.700 --> 01:32.380
or a symbol, except the new line character, which in Python is backslash n.

01:32.400 --> 01:38.310
Knowing the length of the target string, we are specifying the number 285.

01:38.340 --> 01:46.830

00:11.140 --> 00:17.530
The asterisk inside the pattern means that the preceding expression or character should repeat zero

00:17.530 --> 00:23.780
or more times with as many repetitions as possible, meaning it is a greedy repetition.

00:23.800 --> 00:28.090
We are going to discuss greedy versus non greedy behavior very soon.

00:28.090 --> 00:35.350
But for now, just keep in mind that the asterisk is greedy by default and it means zero or more repetitions

00:35.350 --> 00:37.180
of the preceding expression.

00:37.210 --> 00:41.020
Let's see some examples to understand its behavior better.

00:41.050 --> 00:45.310

01:01.540 --> 01:06.010
Each of them representing a digit, followed by the asterisk.

01:06.040 --> 01:12.490
The most important thing to keep in mind here is that the asterisk means zero or more repetitions of

01:12.490 --> 01:14.050
the preceding expression.

01:14.050 --> 01:21.280
And in this case, that expression is the last backslash d over here, not all three of them.

01:21.310 --> 01:28.390
This means that we are basically searching for numbers with two digits and possibly a third digit.

01:28.420 --> 01:35.770
I say possibly because we may not have the third digit meaning zero repetitions according to the asterisk,

01:35.770 --> 01:42.820
or we may have the third digit meaning one repetition of the last backslash D or we may have the fourth

01:42.820 --> 01:46.480
and fifth digit as well, or maybe ten more digits.

01:46.510 --> 01:50.860
There is no upper limit of repetitions enforced by the asterisk.

01:50.860 --> 01:53.490

02:48.440 --> 02:55.370
Next we have the dot asterisk combination, which means that the character represented by the dot may

repeat zero or more times after the capital E.

Also, don't forget what I mentioned at the beginning of this lecture.

The asterisk is greedy, meaning it tries to match as many repetitions of the preceding character as

03:16.970 --> 03:17.840

E after the capital E we may have a character, any character except the new line which repeats zero

00:05.310 --> 00:12.510
Another very useful meta character in regular expression patterns is the pipe or the vertical bar.

00:12.540 --> 00:16.860
The general syntax for this meta character is the following.

00:17.040 --> 00:18.240
A pipe.

00:18.270 --> 00:19.470
B Pipe.

00:19.500 --> 00:24.960
C Where A, B and C are distinct regular expression patterns.

00:24.990 --> 00:29.940
Only one of these patterns is matched either A or B or C.

00:29.970 --> 00:31.230
Not all of them.

00:31.260 --> 00:38.220
The regular expression engine tries these patterns from left to right until one of the patterns has

00:38.220 --> 00:40.500
a match inside the target string.

00:40.530 --> 00:46.110
As soon as that pattern is matched, the rest of the patterns after it will be ignored.

00:46.140 --> 00:53.250
This means that the pipe meta character is not greedy because it resumes to only a single pattern match

00:53.250 --> 00:55.020
from the ones provided.

Now let's see a couple of examples to understand this meta character better.

over here and over here, to chain three different patterns that we want to search for inside the target

01:19.780 --> 01:20.370
string.

01:26.260 --> 01:32.200

00:10.130 --> 00:12.860
syntax used in regular expressions.

00:12.860 --> 00:17.210
And we are going to start by talking about extension notations.

00:17.240 --> 00:23.630
Now, if you remember our discussion on grouping and groups earlier in the course, you should know

00:23.630 --> 00:29.990
that in more complex, regular expression patterns, managing and referencing groups can become quite

00:29.990 --> 00:30.830
difficult.

00:30.860 --> 00:38.150
For instance, imagine having a pattern with 20 or 30 different groups instead of just one or 2 or 3.

00:38.180 --> 00:44.690
As I showed you earlier, in this kind of scenario, the management of a large number of groups can

00:44.690 --> 00:46.000
be a real issue.

00:46.010 --> 00:52.520
So the regular expression syntax allows us to use something called extension notations.

00:52.610 --> 00:59.420
The general syntax for an extension notation is similar to the syntax of a group, meaning we are again

00:59.420 --> 01:00.770
using parentheses.

01:00.800 --> 01:08.160
Only this time we are inserting a question mark right after the opening parentheses, thus signaling

01:08.160 --> 01:14.340
an extension notation since the question mark had no meaning after the opening parentheses of a group

01:14.340 --> 01:21.540
as the first character since it has nothing to repeat, it was chosen as the general syntax for extension

01:21.540 --> 01:22.140
notations.

01:22.140 --> 01:23.840
So let me write this.

01:23.850 --> 01:30.060
So we have open parentheses, the question mark and then the closing parentheses.

01:30.210 --> 01:32.550
This is the general syntax.

01:32.550 --> 01:38.790
The characters that follow the question mark are the ones defining the role and the functionality of

01:38.790 --> 01:40.260
the extension notation.

01:40.260 --> 01:43.410
You can disregard the three dots over here.

01:43.440 --> 01:49.500
They are there only to suggest that other characters are to be added after the question mark.

01:49.620 --> 01:55.890
One thing you can do with such an extension is when you want to match a specific group inside the target

01:55.890 --> 02:02.490
string, but you are not looking to retrieve its contents later using the group or groups method.

02:02.520 --> 02:09.420
This is called a Non-capturing group, meaning the group is matched but it won't be retrieved and used

02:09.420 --> 02:10.560
for anything.

02:10.590 --> 02:11.970
Why is this useful?

02:11.970 --> 02:17.400
Well, returning to our discussion at the beginning of this lecture, when having a large number of

02:17.400 --> 02:23.160
groups in your regular expression pattern, you might want to define even more groups in your pattern

02:23.160 --> 02:28.380
while skipping or ignoring some of the existing groups without deleting them.

02:28.410 --> 02:34.200
The Non-capturing groups will not be retrieved when using the group or groups method.

02:34.200 --> 02:40.140
However, they will still be there for you to maybe reactivate them at a later time.

02:40.140 --> 02:47.160
The syntax for a non-capturing group adds to the general syntax of extension notations by inserting

02:47.160 --> 02:49.860
a colon right after the question mark.

02:49.890 --> 02:57.450
This way we can distinguish between regular capturing groups that can be retrieved later and non-capturing

02:57.450 --> 02:58.140
groups.

02:58.380 --> 03:04.770
Let's take a basic example and see how this kind of groups is ignored by the group and groups.

03:04.770 --> 03:05.640
Methods.

03:10.440 --> 03:15.150

03:26.670 --> 03:27.390

group in the pattern.

So I'm going to use result Dot group of one and we have index group of two for T and group of three

04:40.860 --> 04:42.420
19th February.

Okay, great.

04:50.430 --> 04:51.360
of matches?

04:51.360 --> 04:56.730
Maybe we don't need to retrieve that match for the purposes of our application.

04:56.730 --> 05:02.640
However, since we can change some of the functionality of the application at a later time, perhaps

05:02.640 --> 05:03.930
we want the first group to.

05:04.020 --> 05:07.260
Be maintained in a kind of sleep mode, so to speak.

05:07.290 --> 05:13.500
To do that, we just have to add a question mark, followed by a colon immediately after the opening

05:13.500 --> 05:18.930
parentheses of that group to designate the first group as a non-capturing group.

05:18.960 --> 05:21.450
Let's do this and see the results.

05:21.780 --> 05:29.580
So I'm going to use the same line as above, only this time for the first group, I'm going to add a

05:29.580 --> 05:31.320
question mark and a colon.

05:31.320 --> 05:35.230
And now let's see the results returned by the groups method.

05:35.250 --> 05:38.520
So result dot groups once again.

05:38.550 --> 05:44.910
Notice this time the match corresponding to the first group is not returned anymore since we defined

05:44.910 --> 05:47.100
it as a non-capturing group.

05:47.130 --> 05:49.140
What about the group numbering?

Let's find out with the help of the group method.

So this time I'm going to use result Dot group of one and let's see a result group of two as well.

So this time, since the Non-capturing group has been skipped, Group number one is the first regular

capturing group that is found in the pattern, the one that matches footsy.

06:15.030 --> 06:21.480

06:21.480 --> 06:27.690

Extension notations enable us to work with other useful tools as well, such as assertions which provide

00:12.340 --> 00:16.510
us with even more flexibility when it comes to pattern matching.

00:16.540 --> 00:20.370
There are four types of assertions that I am referring to.

00:20.380 --> 00:27.970
Look ahead and look behind assertions, each of them classified as being either positive or negative.

00:28.000 --> 00:34.060
Although this sounds a bit complicated, we are going to study all four types of assertions, starting

00:34.060 --> 00:36.490
with positive look ahead assertions.

00:36.490 --> 00:42.520
In this lecture, the general syntax for a positive look ahead assertion is the following.

00:42.520 --> 00:47.620
So open parentheses question mark the equal sign.

00:47.650 --> 00:50.920
Then we have a pattern and closing parentheses.

00:50.920 --> 00:54.690
So again, we have the parentheses as we did for groups.

00:54.700 --> 01:01.150
Then inside the parentheses, the first thing we need to enter is the question mark, followed by the

01:01.150 --> 01:02.170
equal sign.

01:02.200 --> 01:08.960
This assertion returns a match only if the following pattern the one which is generally represented

01:08.960 --> 01:12.590
by these three dots over here, matches next.

01:12.590 --> 01:20.010
So in other words, the assertion matches only if it is followed by the pattern after the equal sign.

01:20.030 --> 01:23.120
Let's see a couple of examples to understand this better.

01:23.120 --> 01:28.480
Considering the original target string that we used thus far in the course.

01:28.490 --> 01:30.710
So let me write this.

Okay, so what do we have here?

I assumed that we want to match all the occurrences of the name stocks inside our target string.

So this one over here and also this one over here.

But if and only if it is followed by three consecutive digits.

01:49.490 --> 01:52.430
Therefore, this pattern says the following.

I want to match all five letter words where each letter is uppercase.

01:57.290 --> 02:04.070
Notice the character class over here and the five in between curly braces only if it is followed by

02:04.100 --> 02:06.110
three consecutive digits.

02:06.110 --> 02:13.220
So we have a space and then the pattern representing the three consecutive digits needs to be included

02:13.220 --> 02:15.740
in a positive lookahead assertion.

02:15.740 --> 02:19.910
Notice the parentheses, the question mark and the equal sign.

02:19.910 --> 02:25.940
And then we have the 0 to 9 character class, which represents any digit from 0 to 9, which should

This is due to this backslash s over here being matched as well.

part of the pattern, this one over here in between parentheses.

So let's do this right now.

Open and close parentheses.

04:08.830 --> 04:09.730
billions.

04:09.760 --> 04:17.380
Then we have another sequence of one or more white spaces right here, Backslash s plus right before

04:17.410 --> 04:23.530
the third and last number on each line, which is yet another floating point number corresponding to

04:23.530 --> 04:25.930
the PE ratio value.

04:25.960 --> 04:29.200
Now let me hit enter and see the results.

04:29.860 --> 04:37.480
Okay, so the result is a list of company names for which the revenue is less than 50 billion USD.

And you can double check this result yourself by visually scanning the file and identifying those companies

04:44.740 --> 04:45.640
manually.

04:45.670 --> 04:53.290
Actually, if we look at the file real quick for the revenue, we have three M with $32 Million, so

less than 50.

Then we have Coca Cola with 37, then we have McDonald's with 21, then we have Merck with 46.

Nike with 51.

Then we have Tesla with 24 and finally Visa with 23.

01:22.820 --> 01:28.610
letter and containing at least one uppercase letter, one digit and one special symbol.

We can check if the password provided by the user meets these conditions using regular expression patterns

In the lecture.

Following this video, you will find the template Python script available for download.

this section using the template script.

Requirements.

So first of all, the application is going to ask the user to enter his first name.

02:13.970 --> 02:21.140
The value entered by the user at the prompt needs to meet a certain set of conditions before being considered

02:21.140 --> 02:25.340
valid, and these conditions are stated here in this list.

02:25.340 --> 02:30.860
So the first name should not contain any other characters besides letters.

02:30.860 --> 02:37.850
It should start with a capital letter and continue with all lowercase letters and should be at least

02:37.850 --> 02:44.180
two characters long in case the user's first name is Ed or L, for instance.

02:44.210 --> 02:49.130
Next, the last name should meet the exact same conditions as the first name.

Nothing new here.

people over a certain age to sign up for whatever service we provide.

That's why our application should consider valid.

Only those birthdays starting with January 1st, 2002.

Also, the date of birth should only contain digits and forward slashes following this format right

03:19.490 --> 03:19.820
here.

So we have two digits for the month, a slash, two digits for the day, another slash and then four

03:26.180 --> 03:27.740
digits for the year.

Next, we are asking the user for his or her email address.

03:32.240 --> 03:38.960

03:38.960 --> 03:39.680
valid.

03:39.710 --> 03:47.270
First, it should follow the correct format, which is username at domain dot extension, for instance

03:47.270 --> 03:49.610
jack at gmail.com.

The username should only contain letters, digits, dots or the underscore sign, nothing else.

03:57.350 --> 04:05.540
The domain needs to contain letters only, whilst the extension should consist of 2 to 4 lowercase letters

04:05.540 --> 04:13.910
because we might have domains with two letter extensions such as.us three letter extensions such as.com

04:13.910 --> 04:16.520

04:16.550 --> 04:22.490
Next on our list, the username that the user wants to use for registration.

04:22.910 --> 04:26.060
Maybe we are running a private forum for instance.

04:26.060 --> 04:33.080
The username needs to contain only letters, digits or the underscore character and have a minimum of

04:33.080 --> 04:37.220
six characters in total and a maximum of 12.

04:37.460 --> 04:41.150
Now the fun part the password requirements.

04:41.180 --> 04:47.180
We need to make sure that the user sets a complex and secure password for his or her account.

04:47.180 --> 04:53.060
And this is why we are going to ask for a certain level of complexity in our scenario.

04:53.090 --> 04:56.900
This means that the password should be at least eight characters long.

04:56.930 --> 05:03.800
It should start with a lowercase letter and it must also contain at least one uppercase letter, one

05:03.800 --> 05:04.070
digit.

05:04.210 --> 05:08.800
And one or more of these five special symbols that you see on the screen.

05:08.800 --> 05:12.450
And all of these conditions should be met simultaneously.

05:12.460 --> 05:13.420
Pretty cool.

05:13.570 --> 05:18.260
Next, we are asking the user for his credit card details.

05:18.280 --> 05:21.400
First on the list, the card number itself.

05:21.430 --> 05:25.740
The condition here is that we only accept Visa or Mastercard.

05:25.750 --> 05:33.400
So this means that the card number should start with either 4 or 5, where four signals a visa card

05:33.400 --> 05:35.500
and five is for Mastercard.

05:35.530 --> 05:43.090
We should also make sure that the card number entered by the user is exactly 16 characters long and

05:43.090 --> 05:48.670
consists of nothing but digits, so no spaces or other characters are allowed.

05:49.120 --> 05:54.130
Moving forward, we have the requirements for the credit card expiration date.

05:54.160 --> 06:03.040
In this scenario, the credit card should not expire sooner than May of 2024, so any date beyond that

06:03.040 --> 06:10.550
date is accepted and also the expiration date entered by the user should contain only digits and forward

06:10.550 --> 06:17.030
slashes following this format over here with two digits for the month, a slash and then two digits

06:17.030 --> 06:18.290
for the year.

06:18.320 --> 06:26.180
Finally, we have the card verification code also called card verification value or in short, CVC or

06:26.180 --> 06:26.960
Cvcv.

06:27.470 --> 06:30.350
This simply needs to be a three digit number.

06:30.350 --> 06:36.440
As you may already know, this is usually the number on the back of each card and you are required to

06:36.440 --> 06:39.340
provide it whenever you make online payments.

06:39.350 --> 06:45.890
So these are the requirements for each task that you need to solve for the purpose of this project.

06:45.890 --> 06:52.010
As I mentioned, you can find them after this video along with a few hints that I hope will help you

06:52.010 --> 06:56.210
find the solutions for the most complex tasks in the list.

06:56.300 --> 07:01.820
Before ending this video, let's have a brief look at the template file that you can download from the

07:01.820 --> 07:03.260
next lecture.

07:03.260 --> 07:04.880
And this is it right here.

07:04.880 --> 07:11.420
So for each piece of information that we need to get from the user, we are using the input function

07:11.420 --> 07:18.290
to ask the user for a specific value and then we are saving the information that he enters at the prompt

07:18.320 --> 07:21.140
using the variables that you see here.

07:21.140 --> 07:23.540
For example, f name for the first name.

07:23.630 --> 07:30.050
L name for the last name, date for the date of birth, and so on, on each of the strings that the

07:30.050 --> 07:30.890
user provides.

07:30.890 --> 07:36.560
At the prompt, we are going to perform the pattern matching notice that in between the parentheses

07:36.560 --> 07:43.490
of the full match method over here, there's this empty raw string that waits for you to write a specific

07:43.490 --> 07:44.180
pattern.

07:44.180 --> 07:50.810
Next, for each parameter I have defined an if Elif block of code which prints wrong format.

07:50.810 --> 07:52.130
Please try again.

07:52.130 --> 07:58.730
If your pattern doesn't have a match in the user's input or in other words, if the input entered by

07:58.730 --> 08:04.010
the user does not meet the conditions in your pattern and in the project requirements.

08:04.010 --> 08:09.980
In this case, after printing the error message, the continue statement that you see on the next line

08:09.980 --> 08:17.270
gets the execution back to the top of the while loop and the user is asked for the same input once again

08:17.270 --> 08:20.690
until his or her input meets the conditions.

08:20.900 --> 08:27.260
On the other hand, if the user's input is indeed matching the correct pattern and also the requirements,

08:27.260 --> 08:34.430
then the break statement that you can see under the else clause exits the current while loop and then

08:34.430 --> 08:40.760
the next piece of code is executed and the same mechanism is in place for each piece of information

08:40.760 --> 08:43.010
that we require from the user.

08:43.010 --> 08:49.160
Finally, all the inputs that have been saved from the user, the ones that met the required conditions,

08:49.190 --> 08:52.310
are grouped together inside a list of strings.

08:52.340 --> 08:55.970
This one over here, which I called user info.

08:55.970 --> 09:02.960
And then all the elements of this list are joined together into a single string which is getting printed

09:02.960 --> 09:05.720
out to the screen in the end.

09:05.900 --> 09:08.120
Okay, enough chit chatting for now.

09:08.120 --> 09:14.120
You should go ahead and download the template from the next lecture, read the requirements carefully

and also the provided hints as well, and then get to work.

Start writing your patterns inside the template file.

Test them by running the file in the CMD or the terminal, and if you get stuck at some point you can

With all that said, I wish you good luck and happy coding.

00:04.550 --> 00:10.460
Okay, so I guess you're interested in how I solved each of the tasks in the project requirements.

00:10.460 --> 00:16.910
Meaning how I wrote the regular expression patterns to enforce a set of conditions on each piece of

00:16.910 --> 00:19.930
information that the user enters at the prompt.

00:19.940 --> 00:21.460
So let's get started.

00:21.470 --> 00:27.290
First of all, we need to take care of the pattern that enforces the conditions for the first and last

00:27.320 --> 00:28.520
name of the user.

00:28.520 --> 00:35.210
And we are doing this in these two while loops that you can see over here, this one and this one.

00:35.210 --> 00:41.810
So focusing on the pattern itself, the first letter of each name needs to be an uppercase letter,

00:41.810 --> 00:45.530
hence the capital A to Capital Z character class.

00:45.530 --> 00:51.170
At the beginning of the pattern, following this first character, we have a lowercase letter which

00:51.170 --> 00:52.910
should occur at least once.

00:52.910 --> 01:00.110
So notice the plus sign meta character signaling one or more repetitions of the preceding character,

01:00.110 --> 01:01.880
meaning a lowercase letter.

01:01.880 --> 01:04.410
And that's it for the first and last name.

01:04.410 --> 01:05.900
This was pretty simple.

01:05.910 --> 01:14.010
Next, scrolling down, we have the date of birth, which should be January 1st of 2002 or later.

01:14.010 --> 01:17.760
So this is the while loop covering the date of birth right here.

01:17.760 --> 01:24.720
So we have three areas to focus on the month, which is the first two digits the day, which is the

01:24.720 --> 01:30.960
next two digits in between the forward slashes and finally the year after the second slash.

01:30.960 --> 01:37.980
So let's start with the month since we are starting in January as the lower limit, the month can be

01:37.980 --> 01:40.980
anything from 01212.

01:41.010 --> 01:48.810
So it can be 0102 and so on until zero nine as well as 101 1 or 1 two.

01:48.810 --> 01:54.810
So in between these first pair of parentheses that you see here, we are matching the digits for the

01:54.810 --> 02:02.160
month using the pipe meta character to differentiate between the months starting with zero and the ones

02:02.160 --> 02:03.750
starting with one.

02:03.870 --> 02:11.430
So using character classes, we either have any month from zero one up to zero nine being matched before

02:11.430 --> 02:17.880
the pipe meta character or any month from ten up to 12 being matched after the pipe.

02:18.000 --> 02:24.600
Then we have the forward slash that you can see over here in the pattern before the digits representing

02:24.600 --> 02:26.250
the day of the month.

02:26.250 --> 02:30.840
Again, we are matching any of the days from zero 1 to 0 nine.

02:30.930 --> 02:32.850
Over here before the pipe.

02:32.850 --> 02:37.890
Then we are matching the days from ten up to 29 over here.

02:37.920 --> 02:44.700
Notice this character set, meaning 1 or 2 followed by a backslash D meaning any digit.

02:44.700 --> 02:51.810
And finally, after the second pipe right here, we have a three followed by the zero one character

02:51.810 --> 02:56.810
set, which matches days 30 or 31 of the month.

02:56.820 --> 03:03.690
Next we have the second slash right here following this slash, we should have the year again.

03:03.690 --> 03:13.530
I used the pipe to provide two possible matches here either any year from 2002 until 2009 or any year

03:13.530 --> 03:17.970
from 2010 up to 2099.

03:18.150 --> 03:24.900
And this way we are covering all possible scenarios regarding the date, meaning any date, which is

03:24.900 --> 03:29.520
January 1st, 2002, or a subsequent date.

03:30.180 --> 03:30.930
Okay.

03:30.930 --> 03:37.020
Now let's move on and scroll down to check out the code for the email address.

03:37.140 --> 03:43.320
This should follow the format described in the project requirements, so the username part of the email

03:43.320 --> 03:49.260
address may contain only letters, digits, dots or the underscore character.

03:49.260 --> 03:52.830
So inside our pattern, using the pipe meta character.

03:52.830 --> 04:00.600
Once again, I have defined all the characters that are allowed before the at symbol, either the backslash

04:00.600 --> 04:07.260
w special sequence which covers letters digits and the underscore symbol or the actual dot.

04:07.290 --> 04:14.880
Notice that I used the backslash to escape this dot and differentiate it from the dot meta character.

04:14.880 --> 04:19.680
Any of the characters surrounding the pipe may repeat one or more times.

04:19.710 --> 04:25.740
Notice the plus sign over here taking care of this condition being met as well.

04:25.830 --> 04:28.350
Next we have the at symbol itself.

04:28.350 --> 04:34.950
From each email address and following this symbol, we have the domain name of the email provider.

04:34.950 --> 04:41.100
According to our project's specifications, this domain name should contain only lowercase letters,

04:41.130 --> 04:48.540
hence the lowercase A to lowercase Z character class and the plus sign meta character over here.

04:48.540 --> 04:56.100
Finally, the extension should be all lowercase letters and should consist of 2 to 4 characters only.

04:56.100 --> 05:04.020
Again, we have the A to Z character class, followed by a pair of curly braces with two and four as.

05:04.060 --> 05:07.780
The lower and upper limits separated by a comma.

05:07.780 --> 05:09.640
And this is the email address.

05:09.670 --> 05:10.350
Good.

05:10.360 --> 05:12.760
Now let's move on to the username.

05:12.760 --> 05:18.130
So this piece of code right here, this is a pattern that should be easy to write.

05:18.130 --> 05:25.720
The username must contain only letters, digits or the underscore sign, nothing else besides these.

05:25.720 --> 05:32.350
Also, the length of the username must be between 6 and 12 characters, and that's exactly what our

05:32.350 --> 05:34.210
pattern is going to match.

05:34.210 --> 05:41.200
So we have the backslash w special sequence followed by a pair of curly braces containing the limits

05:41.230 --> 05:43.180
six and 12.

05:44.040 --> 05:47.340
Okay, next we have the code for the password.

05:47.340 --> 05:53.230
And if you solve this yourself, you are already an advanced user of regular expressions.

05:53.250 --> 05:54.900
If not, then don't worry.

05:54.900 --> 05:58.200
This is a great chance for you to learn and improve.

05:58.230 --> 06:03.240
So first of all, let's take a look at the password requirements once again.

06:03.240 --> 06:08.370
We must have at least eight characters, so this means eight or more.

06:08.400 --> 06:12.840
Secondly, the password must begin with a lowercase letter.

06:12.840 --> 06:19.020
And finally, the complexity of the password should be high, meaning it needs to have at least an uppercase

06:19.020 --> 06:24.900
letter, a digit and a special symbol in order to be considered valid and secure.

06:24.930 --> 06:31.920
The five special symbols that can be part of the user password in our scenario are these five defined

06:31.920 --> 06:35.160
in the project requirements list over here.

06:35.160 --> 06:39.860
So let's analyze the pattern that I wrote in my project file.

06:39.870 --> 06:46.630
So first we need the password to begin with a lowercase letter, hence the carrot, which always matches

06:46.630 --> 06:51.670
at the beginning of the string and the lowercase A to lowercase Z character class.

06:51.760 --> 06:56.530
Next we have a collection of four positive lookahead assertions.

06:56.530 --> 07:04.060
So these four right here that enforce for different conditions, as you may recall from earlier in the

07:04.060 --> 07:10.600
course, with the help of a positive lookahead assertion, the pattern before the assertion is matched,

07:10.630 --> 07:16.690
if and only if, the pattern inside the parentheses of the assertion follows next.

07:16.720 --> 07:17.320
Okay.

07:17.320 --> 07:22.180
With this in mind, let's take a closer look at the first Lookahead assertion.

07:22.180 --> 07:28.030
So that would be this one right here after the specific syntax, which is a question mark, followed

07:28.030 --> 07:29.440
by the equals sign.

07:29.440 --> 07:37.900
We have the meta character right here, followed by a seven and a comma in between curly braces.

07:37.900 --> 07:40.780
How to translate this into plain English?

07:40.780 --> 07:48.730
Well, match the pattern outside the assertion if and only if it is followed by at least seven other

07:48.730 --> 07:49.510
characters.

07:49.510 --> 07:52.450
Any characters except the new line?

07:52.450 --> 07:54.430
Pretty straightforward, I think so.

07:54.430 --> 07:57.910
This is how the password length condition is enforced.

07:58.360 --> 08:04.330
Now the next condition, and that is the password must contain at least an uppercase letter.

08:04.720 --> 08:13.060
So we have a dot and the asterisk meta characters followed by the capital A to Capital Z character class

08:13.060 --> 08:13.990
over here.

08:14.080 --> 08:21.340
This translates to the following logic Match the pattern outside the assertion if and only if it is

08:21.340 --> 08:27.190
followed by an uppercase letter, either immediately after the first character, which is the lowercase

08:27.190 --> 08:33.310
letter at the beginning of the password, or if there are other characters in between the first letter

08:33.310 --> 08:35.500
and the uppercase letter.

08:35.500 --> 08:42.280
So no matter if this uppercase letter is the second letter in the password or there are other characters

08:42.280 --> 08:48.250
between the first letter and the uppercase letter, this uppercase letter should exist somewhere in

08:48.250 --> 08:51.640
the password, regardless of its actual location.

08:51.640 --> 08:56.590
The same logic applies to the next two conditions as well the one for the digit.

08:56.590 --> 09:03.850
So we have backslash D over here as well as the one for the special symbol right here.

09:03.850 --> 09:10.570
So no matter if other characters precede any of these required characters, they still need to follow

09:10.570 --> 09:14.890
the first character in the password, which is the lowercase letter.

09:15.070 --> 09:22.270
Okay, so putting all of this together, we might translate this syntax like this, match the pattern

09:22.270 --> 09:29.770
outside the assertions, if and only if, that pattern, the lowercase letter is being followed by an

09:29.770 --> 09:35.560
uppercase letter, a digit and a special symbol wherever they are in the string.

09:35.560 --> 09:38.440
We just want to make sure that they are there.

09:38.440 --> 09:45.490
Finally, the password may contain any of these characters one or several times until the end of the

09:45.490 --> 09:47.560
string, until the end of the password.

09:47.560 --> 09:54.400
And that is signaled by this long character class that I have highlighted here, followed by the plus

09:54.400 --> 09:57.490
sign meta character at the end of the pattern.

09:57.730 --> 10:04.810
Okay, next we have the credit card number and this is covered by this piece of code right here.

10:04.930 --> 10:12.250
The credit card number needs to be a string of exactly 16 consecutive digits, starting with either

10:12.250 --> 10:15.880
four for Visa or five for Mastercard.

10:15.910 --> 10:18.190
The pattern is a very simple one.

10:18.190 --> 10:21.090
The string starts with either 4 or 5.

10:21.100 --> 10:29.170
Notice this group over here and the use of the pipe meta character followed by 15 other digits, any

10:29.170 --> 10:31.030
digits from 0 to 9.

10:31.030 --> 10:37.390
So we have the backslash D special sequence followed by 15 in between curly braces.

10:37.900 --> 10:41.050
Okay, moving forward, let's scroll down a bit.

10:41.080 --> 10:43.240
We have the expiration date.

10:43.360 --> 10:47.190
Of the cart covered by this piece of code right here.

10:47.200 --> 10:54.900
So considering the requirements of the project, this date should not be sooner than May of 2024.

10:54.910 --> 11:01.390
So again, using character classes and the pipe meta character, we are using a similar logic to the

11:01.390 --> 11:03.880
one we used for the date of birth.

11:03.880 --> 11:06.040
We can split this in two.

11:06.070 --> 11:14.410
First, we should match the rest of the months in 2024 and then all the dates from 2025 onwards.

11:14.410 --> 11:24.280
So first we have months zero 5 to 0 nine or 10 to 12 of year 2024 or just 24 in our case.

11:24.280 --> 11:32.800
Right then after this pipe meta character right here, we are matching any month from zero 1 to 1 two
